<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="" /></noinclude><section begin=par130 />{{GHGmargin-letter|130|g}}
(6) The numeral {{GHGheb|text=אַחַד|translate=one}} for {{GHGheb|text=אֶחָד}} in close connexion, and even with small disjunctives, e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=3|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=48|verse=22|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=9|verse=3}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=17|verse=22}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=27|verse=12}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=11|verse=7}}.

The character of these passages shows that the numeral here cannot be in the construct state, but is merely a rhythmical shortening of the usual (tone-lengthened) form.<section end=par130 />

<section begin=par131 />{{GHGpar-heading|131|Apposition}}

{{GHGmargin-letter|131|a}}
'''1.''' Apposition in the stricter sense is the collocation of two substantives in the same case in order to define more exactly (or to complete) the one by the other, and, as a rule (see, however, below, under ''g''), the former by the latter. Apposition in Hebrew (as in the other Semitic languages<ref>On certain uses of apposition peculiar to the Semitic languages, cf. the exhaustive discussion by Fleischer, ‘Ueber einige Arten der Nominalapposition im Arab.’ (''Kleine Schriften'', ii. 16); [and see also Driver, {{GHGcite|title=Tenses}}, Appendix IV.]</ref>) is by no means confined to those cases in which it is used in English or in the classical languages. It is not infrequently found when either the ''subordination'' of one substantive to the other or some more circumstantial kind of epexegetical addition would be expected.

'''2.''' The principal kinds of apposition in Hebrew are:—

{{GHGmargin-letter|131|b}}
(''a'') The collocation of ''genus'' and ''species'', e.g. {{GHGheb|text=אִשָּׁה אַלְמָנָה|translate=a woman}} (who was) ''a widow'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=7|verse=14}}; {{GHGheb|text=נַֽעֲרָה בְתוּלָה|translate=a damsel}} (that is) ''a virgin'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Dt|chapter=22|verse=23}}, 28, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=4|verse=4}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=19|verse=1|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ju|chapter=21|verse=12|hidebook=1}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=30|verse=17}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=1|verse=2}}; cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=13|verse=8}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Gn|chapter=21|verse=20|hidebook=1}} (where, however, {{GHGheb|text=קַשָּׁת}} is probably an explanatory gloss); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ex|chapter=24|verse=5}} ({{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=11|verse=15}}), {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=15|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=3|verse=16}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=5|verse=29|hidebook=1}} (but probably {{GHGheb|text=סֵ֫בֶל}} should be read instead of {{GHGheb|text=סַבָּל}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Is|chapter=3|verse=24}} (unless {{GHGheb|text=מַֽעֲשֵׂה}} is to be read), {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jer|chapter=20|verse=1}}. Perhaps also {{GHGheb|text=כֹּהֵן הָרֹאשׁ|translate=the priest}} (who is) ''the chief man'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 K|chapter=25|verse=18}}, &c.; others take {{GHGheb|text=כֹּהֵן}} as constr. st.—In {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 S|chapter=10|verse=7}} read {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־צְבָא הַגִּבּ׳}} with the LXX, as in the parallel passage {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 Ch|chapter=19|verse=9}} for {{GHGheb|text=כָּל־צָבָא הַגּ׳}}, which is evidently meant to refer to the reading in 2 S.

{{GHGmargin-letter|131|c}}
(''b'') Collocation of the ''person'' or ''thing'' and the ''attribute'', e.g. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=20|verse=29}} (27:13) {{GHGheb|text=זֶה חֵ֫לֶק־אָדָם רָשָׁע|translate=this is the portion of a man}}, (who is) ''a wicked man'' (but {{GHGheb|text=רָשָׁע}} might also be an adject.); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=6|verse=12}}.—{{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=6|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Lv|chapter=16|verse=4|hidebook=1}} (where, however, {{GHGheb|text=קֹ֫דֶשׁ}} is probably a gloss); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Pr|chapter=22|verse=21}} {{GHGheb|text=אֲמָרִים אֱמֶת|translate=words}} (which are) ''truth''; (immediately after {{GHGheb|text=אִמְרֵי אֱמֶת}}) cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 S|chapter=2|verse=13}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Mi|chapter=1|verse=11}} (where, however, {{GHGheb|text=בּ֫שֶׁת}} is most probably a gloss on {{GHGheb|text=עֶרְיָה}}); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Zc|chapter=1|verse=13}} (=''comfortable words''); {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=45|verse=5}} (?) 68:17 (cf. verse 16). In a wider sense this includes also such cases as {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=60|verse=5}} {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫יִן תַּרְעֵלָה|translate=wine}} which is ''staggering'' (intoxicating drink), which causes staggering<ref>Unless it is to be translated ''thou gavest us intoxication to drink as wine'' (and so in {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=27}} ''give him affliction to eat as bread'', &c.); cf. {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=80|verse=6}} and the analogous examples of apposition in the form of a second accusative in {{GHGpar|117|kk}}. Moreover, having regard to {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫יִן הָרֶ֫קַח|translate=spiced wine}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ct|chapter=8|verse=2}}, and {{GHGheb|text=עַ֫יִר פֶּ֫רֶא}} ''a wild ass’s colt'', {{GHGbible-ref|book=Jb|chapter=11|verse=12}} (in which passages {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫יִן}} and {{GHGheb|text=עַ֫יִר}} must certainly be in the construct state) we cannot but ask whether the Masora does not intend the {{GHGheb|text=יַ֫יִן}} in {{GHGbible-ref|book=Ps|chapter=60|verse=5}} to be taken as construct state (for which elsewhere {{GHGheb|text=יֵין}}).</ref>; {{GHGbible-ref|book=1 K|chapter=22|verse=27}}, {{GHGbible-ref|book=2 Ch|chapter=18|verse=26}} {{GHGheb|text=מַ֫יִם לַ֫חַץ}} (in<section end=par131 /><noinclude>
<references/></noinclude>
